## Literature review

This was already somehow handled for PE with stellar mass binaries with LISA, e.g. 

- [this paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.08544.pdf), with a very useful discussion of the $\mathcal{M}_{c}$ - $\eta$ degeneracy, although for them the frequency variation is very small. 
- or [this one](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.00357.pdf) (Mersat, Baker, Dal Canton).

The merger time is not a good parameter to do PE, it degenerates with the chirp mass a lot.
One can instead do PE with a time at some fixed frequency, which can be optimized.

Inspiration for a way to do multibanding, perhaps?

Independent group tackling the same problem: [Buscicchio+](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.05259.pdf) in Birmingham.

## LGWA parameter estimation

### Source selection

We elect to start the exploration of the capabilities of the LGWA by injecting into it parameters from the two most famous detectections from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration:

- GW150914, the first detection, a binary of black holes with component masses around $30M_{\odot}$;
- GW170817, the first neutron star binary detection, with component masses around $1.4M_{\odot}$, whose electromagnetic counterpart was detected from the radio band up to the GigaelectronVolt.

In order to select a single set of parameters from the posterior distributions of these sources, we compute the signal-to-noise ratio they would have if detected by the LGWA for each posterior sample.

We expect the sources detected by the LVK to be typically located in sky directions favorable for it, which will not coincide with those favorable for the LGWA. On the other hand, the intrinsic distribution of the astrophysical population is expected to be roughly isotropic, as all these sources are extragalactic.
Therefore, we randomize the sky position of the source and perform the same computation, choosing the injection parameters as those yielding the median of this distribution.

### General injection results

### Geometry of lunar time measurement

The "time" parameter we use during parameter estimation is the time of merger, computed at a point we choose to be the location of the Moon as it receives the merger signal.

The scale of the uncertainty in merger time is quite small (less than a second), so assuming this to be known is not a significant approximation - even in real PE, we will be able to choose a fiducial reference frame to within a really good approximation.

Our reference frame is a rigid shift of the ICRS frame to the new coordinate center; as the source is for all intents and purposes infinitely far away we can still use right ascension and declination as coordinates.

Let us consider this frame as fixed.
The other assumption we are making is that the parameter is the time of merger; however, the merger does not actually happen in band for LGWA, therefore we are driven to ask if there is a better way.

We can define the time at frequency $f$ as 

$$
t(f) = t_\text{mrg} + \underbrace{ \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{\text{d}\varphi(f; \theta)}{\text{d}f} }_{ \text{time to merger} }\,,
$$

where the phase $\varphi(f, \theta)$ is the one from the frequency-domain waveform, computed at 3.5PN order.
Is this parameter better measured than the time of merger for some frequencies? Yes, as the following figure shows: 


We can see that the standard deviation of $t(f)$ has a minimum at a frequency within the band of LGWA, below 1Hz.
